title: Love the Hard Way
full_review:
A promising young medical student falls for a two-bit hustler and is dragged down by the undertow of his self-destructive lifestyle in the depressingly acidic drama, "Love the Hard Way" (Kino).

Based on a work by Chinese novelist Wang Shuo and boasting a strong lead performance by Academy Award winner Adrien Brody, director Peter Sehr's bleak take on relationships is weighed down by a near-toxic pessimism that makes viewing it about as edifying as a post-mortem.

Jack (Brody) is a self-confessed student of the streets, "majoring in pimping and petty blackmail." Along with his partner in crime, Charlie (Jon Seda), he runs a lucrative sting, swindling foreign businessmen in fake vice raids -- a well-oiled scam which involves two hired floozies posing as hookers, while Jack and Charlie play the parts of dirty cops who gladly accept "donations" to the Police Benevolent Association in exchange for a slap on the wrist. Jack, who struts through the film with a snakeskin braggadocio and matching jacket, is also a connoisseur of rare first editions and a closet pulp novelist.

Claire (Charlotte Ayanna) is a book-wormish pre-med student at Columbia University, who works part time at the concession stand of a downtown movie theatre which Jack frequents. She finds his bad-boy charm and roguish mystique intriguing and agrees to let him take her to dinner. Over drinks, Jack regurgitates such stale rebel-without-a-cause aphorisms as, "I don't like people who think they know anything because they read a few books ... I'm big on experience." Apparently, his tired iconoclastic claptrap -- not to mention his dubious claims of having bedded more than 200 women -- has an aphrodisiac effect on Claire and the two head back to his place for a rapturous nightcap. She promptly jettisons her Ivy-League beau and goal-oriented ambitions, as she begins her downward spiral from attraction to obsession.

One glaring narrative pothole never satisfactorily filled is why Claire, who is presented as being deeply engrossed by her studies, would show any interest in -- let alone fall head over heels for -- such a scoundrel; high SAT scores can only account for academic aptitude and have little to say concerning good sense.

Jack, who hides his vulnerability behind killer shades and a too-hip-to-care sneer, is incapable of love, let alone commitment. As one of his stooges explains to a distraught Claire, "You're a foreign body in his world ... foreign bodies get rejected." Yet Jack can con everyone but himself. Unable to come to terms with the reality of his emotions for Claire -- the only glimmer of hope in his otherwise dead-end existence -- he creates fiction, telling her that she was just another sexual conquest.

The film plummets along with Claire from depression to despair as she, after finding him in bed with another woman, stumbles headlong into the headlights of her own self-destruction. The bottom falls out when Jack bursts into a seedy hotel room during one of his mock raids, only to find Claire engaging in sex with a seedy patron, sending his once self-assured world into a tailspin of rage and emotional impotency.

Though at times difficult to watch, the film raises important questions about emotional dependency and disconnectedness. Unfortunately, in exploring these themes, the filmmaker seems resigned to limit his palette to just two colors -- soot grey and pitch black. The inner landscape of these emotional cripples is a barren desert devoid of any hope in redemption and scorched by a paralyzing, almost systemic, nihilism. The only bones tossed to the dogs of optimism are foiled by mawkish melodrama, as in the film's final line spoken by Claire to Jack, "You're gonna do what all good writers do -- write a new book." Of course, there is no guarantee that it will have any rosier an ending.

Compounding the alienating gloom is a debasing view of sexual intimacy, in which, in addition to being a recreational sport, sex is portrayed as an effective means of inflicting pain on others, as well as the weapon of choice for self-mutilation, as in the case of Claire's fall into self-loathing.

Due to recurring sexual encounters with nudity, some violence, much rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
